newsitem.title: USA: Two Republicans seen as potential US FERC nominee.
newsitem.headline: Two Republicans seen as potential US FERC nominee.

text.p: Two Republicans emerged at the top of the list of possible nominees to replace Donald Santa on the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, natural gas and electric industry sources said Friday.

Industry officials said the complexion of the commission could shift sharply with Santa due to step down at the end of his term in June, and chairwoman Elizabeth Moler tapped Thursday to be Deputy Energy Secretary.
Curt Hebert, chairman of the Mississippi Public Service Commission, and McLane Layton, an aide to Sen. Don Nickles of Oklahoma, were considered to have the inside track to replace Santa.

Hebert has Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi backing him, and Layton has Nickles, the number two Republican and a member of the Senate Energy Committee which has to approve FERC appointments, behind her.
Hebert said Friday he was aware he might be under consideration.
"It's hard to say how these things play out when they're considering you," he said, adding that he would be interested in the job if offered.
A spokesman for Nickles said there have "some discussions" about recommending Layton, but declined to elaborate on who was involved in the discussions.
"She's well qualified and very knowledgable on these issues," he said.
Gas industry officials saw Layton as a known quantity which they favored, while conservative electric utilities were pushing Hebert's name.
Mississippi is among the states which is considered least likely to promote the break up of utility monopolies, since the state has low electric rates and could see prices go up in an open market.
"(Hebert) is very much of a states' rights advocate," said a spokesman for Southern Company, which owns Mississippi Power. "That's certainly the position Southern Co takes also."
Industry officials widely expected FERC commissioner William Massey or commissioner James Hoecker to be named to replace Moler at the helm.
"It's too complicated and difficult an agency for an outsider to walk in and lead," said one Washington lawyer.
Sources said if Massey or Hoecker took the reins, the commission might lean more toward an activist role, using its regulatory power to push the electric deregulation agenda.

Contrasting Santa's approach toward electric utility mergers versus the other commissioners, one lawyer said Massey and Hoecker may be more likely to use merger cases to advance the goal of making utilities divest their generation assets to promote competitive power markets.
Massey and Hoecker are both Democrats, as is Moler, while Santa is an independent. Under commission rules, no more than three commissioners may be from the same political party.
Industry officials were more hardpressed to come up with ideas for filling a Democratic slot on the commission.
Texas public utility commissioner Robert Gee, who was considered by President Clinton for a spot on the commission four years ago, would be an obvious choice, sources said.
